vignette:
Kofi Mensah is a 22-year-old man of Ghanaian descent who works as a school principal - a role he took on with unusual intensity, driven, he has said, by a need to be the kind of authority figure he never had as a child. He grew up in a household defined by his caregiver's volatility: beatings that came without warning, triggered by nothing Kofi could ever reliably identify. The unpredictability was its own particular cruelty. A good morning could end with a belt. A quiet evening could end with worse. By the time he was a teenager, Kofi had learned to read rooms the way other children read books - scanning for shifts in posture, tone, the particular silence that preceded violence. That vigilance kept him functional, but it never left him.

He sought help recently, at 22, after an incident at school that frightened him deeply. A student had been defiant, and Kofi had felt a surge of rage so sudden and so total that he had to leave the room. He stood in the hallway, shaking, convinced he had been about to do something he could not take back. He has come to believe, with a certainty that feels immovable, that he carries something broken inside him - that the abuse has permanently altered his character, that the capacity for violence was installed in him during childhood and now waits. The fear that he will lose control and do something terrible is not a passing worry; it is the organizing principle of his inner life. And it is this very appraisal - that he is damaged, dangerous, and unable to stop bad things from unfolding - that keeps pulling him back toward the trauma, as though his mind is searching the past for evidence that might either confirm or finally disprove what he fears about himself.

The memories themselves are difficult to work with. When Kofi tries deliberately to recall what happened to him, he finds the material strangely inaccessible - he reaches for it and finds gaps, white space, a sense of something just out of reach. What he does have comes in disconnected pieces: the texture of a particular floor, the sound of a door, a fragment of a voice - none of it forming a coherent sequence. Yet these same memories, when they arrive uninvited, feel more vivid and present than anything in his current life. They do not feel like the past. This quality - the way involuntary recall carries a sensory immediacy that deliberate recall cannot access - has itself become a source of dread, reinforcing his belief that he is not in control of his own mind, that he is permanently changed, that something fundamental was taken from him and cannot be restored.

Certain things reliably pull these fragments to the surface. Old photographs - particularly ones from his childhood - can drop him without warning into sensory material he cannot fully reconstruct but cannot escape. Waking from a nightmare leaves him suspended in a state where the residue of the dream and the fragments of actual memory blur together, and for long minutes he cannot locate himself in the present. These intrusions, in turn, deepen his conviction that he is helpless - that bad things will keep happening to him regardless of what he does - and that helplessness then lowers his threshold for the next intrusion, as though the appraisal itself sensitizes him to triggers he might otherwise weather.

What makes his occupational life particularly fraught is that schools are, by their nature, unpredictable environments. A sudden argument in a hallway, a raised voice, an unexpected knock on his office door - any of these can function as the kind of environmental ambiguity that his nervous system was trained to treat as threat. In those moments, the fragments return, the fear of his own rage rises, and Kofi finds himself managing his students and staff from behind a wall of careful, exhausting control.

He came to therapy, finally, because he is in a relationship with someone he loves and is afraid of what he might become. What he hopes for, tentatively, is to stop feeling like a danger to the people around him. What he fears most is that therapy will confirm what he already suspects - that the damage is real, and permanent, and his.
